### Overall Assessment: Treat with Caution

Cristancho and colleagues ask a question the community-violence literature had not put to data: does a homicide near an early-childhood center degrade the observed quality of what happens inside the classroom? Their answer comes from a two-wave (May and November 2019) panel of 298 low-income children in 52 classrooms across 43 publicly funded providers in Bogotá and Cartagena, matched to geocoded police homicide records and estimated with child or classroom fixed effects, which with two waves is a first-differences design (p.5). The child-level half of the paper is the reliable half: an additional homicide within 500 m in the 7 days before assessment lowers emergent numeracy by 0.35 SD and emergent literacy/language by 0.28 SD (Table 2, cols. 1–2), effects that are large but directionally consistent with the acute-exposure literature the paper cites and that fade at longer windows as that literature would predict. The classroom-level half, which is the paper's reason for existing, is not yet evidence the field should build on. The headline −0.53 SD effect on pedagogical quality (Table 2, col. 6) is a borderline estimate (SE 0.26 in the table, 0.25 in the text; p = .04) from 102 classroom-wave observations, and the number of classrooms that actually change exposure status between waves is never reported in the article (the only switcher count given is 60 children at the 14-day window, p.5). More seriously, the paper's own balance table undercuts its own balance narrative: the text says exposed–unexposed differences are "substantially reduced" once fixed effects are applied (p.4), but Table 1 shows that within the same unit, exposed waves have markedly less-educated teachers (FE-adjusted −0.47*** and −0.36***) and fewer learning materials (−0.63* and −0.84***), differences that are larger than the unadjusted ones and that sit exactly on the variables most likely to move an observation-based quality rating. Whether that reflects teacher turnover caused by violence (a mediator) or coincidental staffing changes in a handful of treated centers (a confounder), it means the classroom estimate cannot be read as the effect of a homicide on how a given teacher teaches. The "detectable up to 6 weeks" claim rests on cumulative windows ("homicides within X days," each on its own buffered sample) misdescribed as lagged effects, with the 21-day estimate not significant (Figure 3); the abstract's child-effect range "–.14 SD to –.35 SD" includes a null motor estimate and omits a positive executive-function estimate that becomes significantly positive at 3, 4, and 6 weeks; two of fifteen future-homicide placebos are significant (Figure 2, +14 days, numeracy and executive function) where the text says they are "not consistently predictive"; and the heterogeneity result the abstract advertises rests on an appendix table with no numbers in the article, which the authors themselves call non-causal (p.10). There is no code, no software statement, and no derivation of the headline Ns (557 and 102). The right posture for the field is this: cite the paper for the numeracy and literacy replication in Colombian preschoolers and for having opened the classroom-quality question with a first, fragile estimate; do not cite it for an established effect size on classroom quality, for six-week persistence, for protective factors, or for classroom quality as a mechanism, until a larger sample with more waves and a transparent treatment of within-unit staffing changes confirms it. A reader who weights the child-level corroboration more heavily than the classroom headline could reasonably land one notch higher; we do not, because the classroom claim is what the paper will be cited for.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** Two wording corrections. Only the two 7-day cells flip sign (learning materials 0.51* → −0.63*; teacher higher education 0.24** → −0.47***); the 14-day cells keep their sign and grow (−0.60*** → −0.84***; −0.17* → −0.36***). And the p. 4 sentence names crime exposure and demographics, for which "substantially reduced" is true (the crime rows shrink from 1.24***, 0.77*** and 1.11*** to 0.07, 0.23* and −0.03, and the demographic rows go to about zero); it does not name learning materials or teacher education, so it is incomplete rather than wrong, which is how the Codex review read it. The within-unit imbalance on those two rows is real and the concern about the classroom estimate stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table.

#### Key Strengths

- The question is new and well-chosen. Prior quasi-experimental work on acute violence exposure measures children (test scores, attention, regulation) or administrative school functioning (teacher absence, principal turnover); none had used a structured classroom-observation instrument as the outcome. Moving the unit of analysis from the child to the setting is the right next step for a literature that wants to say something about intervention, and the paper deserves credit for it.
- The data combination is unusual and fit for purpose: direct child assessment (IDELA, five domains, α = .58–.79), observer-rated process quality (IMCEIC, nine items, α = .72), and day-level, geocoded police homicide records at multiple radii (pp.4–5). Few datasets link all three.
- The design is transparent and its checks are the standard ones done properly: the identifying assumption is stated (p.6); the chronic-exposure control is built so it cannot overlap the shock window; a one-week buffer sharpens the treated/untreated contrast; future homicides (+7, +14, +21) serve as placebos in the same panel as the treatment windows; radii and a non-violent-crime comparison are run (appendix only). Figures 3 and 4 label every point estimate, so the classroom results are checkable from the page.
- The 7-day child results are credible and coherent with the field. Numeracy (−0.35***) and literacy (−0.28**) are significant at the shortest window and null thereafter, which is the temporal signature the acute-exposure literature reports, and the Figure 2 significance markers at −7 days agree with Table 2.
- The authors concede a good deal in the Discussion and Limitations: small N and low power (p.10), residual imbalance (p.11), no pre-trend test with two waves (p.11), inability to separate center from home exposure (pp.10–11), and non-random moderators (p.10). The concessions are real; the problem is that they do not travel to the abstract or Conclusions.

#### Key Concerns

- The classroom-quality headline is identified from very little variation, and the paper does not say how little. With about 5.7 analytic children per classroom, the 60 child switchers at 14 days (p.5) imply on the order of ten switching classrooms (an inference; the count is in unavailable Appendix Table 5). The estimate is t ≈ 2.0, the 95% CI runs from about −1.04 to −0.02, and inference clusters on 43 providers with few treated clusters and no small-cluster correction reported.
- Within-unit imbalance on teacher education and learning materials contradicts the text and threatens the classroom estimate directly. Table 1's FE-adjusted differences for these rows are larger than the unadjusted ones and flip sign (learning materials 0.51* → −0.63* at 7 days, −0.60*** → −0.84*** at 14 days; teacher higher education 0.24** → −0.47***, −0.17* → −0.36***). Under child fixed effects a nonzero FE-adjusted difference is possible only if the variable changed between waves, so exposed waves coincide with staffing or materials changes. The child models do not control for these; the classroom model includes unnamed "center-level structural quality indicators" (p.5). The text's "substantially reduced" (p.4) does not describe these rows.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Two wording corrections. Only the two 7-day cells flip sign (learning materials 0.51* → −0.63*; teacher higher education 0.24** → −0.47***); the 14-day cells keep their sign and grow (−0.60*** → −0.84***; −0.17* → −0.36***). And the p. 4 sentence names crime exposure and demographics, for which "substantially reduced" is true (the crime rows shrink from 1.24***, 0.77*** and 1.11*** to 0.07, 0.23* and −0.03, and the demographic rows go to about zero); it does not name learning materials or teacher education, so it is incomplete rather than wrong, which is how the Codex review read it. The within-unit imbalance on those two rows is real and the concern about the classroom estimate stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table.

- Cumulative windows are narrated as persistence. Shocks are "homicides within X days" (Table 2 note a), each window on a different buffered sample, so a significant 42-day coefficient re-detects recent events rather than showing that a six-week-old homicide still matters. The 21-day pedagogical-quality estimate (−0.47) is not significant; the socio-emotional profile is non-monotonic (significant at 7, 21, 28, 35 days; null at 14 and 42), and the Results (p.7: "within 35 days") and Discussion (p.10: "up to 42 days, –0.11 to –0.33") describe it differently, with the Discussion version contradicted by Figure 2.
- The prose repeatedly reads the exhibits more favorably than they warrant. The abstract's "ds = –.14 SD to –.35 SD" folds in a null (motor, p = .27) and omits executive functions (+0.12, and +0.18 to +0.22 and significant at 21, 28, and 42 days, against the hypothesis). "Not consistently predictive" placebos (p.7) include two significant +14-day coefficients. The motor null is said to "match our initial hypothesis" (p.10) when p.2 predicted negative effects generally. The Conclusions' "classroom quality may be a mechanism" (p.11) is not tested: child and classroom effects are estimated on different windows (7 vs. 14 days), no mediation analysis exists, and the Discussion's own timing argument (p.10) points to immediate stress responses rather than instructional loss.
- Verification is largely impossible from the article. No code, no software statement, no sample-flow arithmetic (298 × 2 = 596 vs. N = 557; 52 × 2 = 104 vs. N = 102), no statement of whether outcomes are standardized within wave or how "months between collections" is coded (its Table 1 cells are blank, suggesting it is constant within child and absorbed by the fixed effect, leaving nothing to absorb May-to-November growth). The attrition analysis, switcher counts, heterogeneity, radius, and robbery results all live in a supplement whose numbers never appear in the text, and the robbery result is described four incompatible ways (pp.6, 9, 10, 11).
- The literature framing overstates the gap and mischaracterizes several sources. "Little evidence on mechanisms" (p.9) ignores causal work on school-functioning channels (Monteiro & Rocha 2017 is cited but underused; Jarillo et al. 2016 and Laurito et al. 2019 are not cited). Ang (2021) concerns police killings measured from students' homes, not homicides near centers (the paper's own reference title says so, p.12). Abufhele & Laurito (2023) measure municipality-level, not near-home, exposure. The lead author's own Cristancho et al. (2024), which set the 7-day/500 m specification and found effects roughly a third the size, is cited only inside citation strings and never compared.

#### What to Rely On

- Directionally, an additional homicide within 500 m of the provider in the week before assessment lowers young children's emergent numeracy and emergent literacy/language scores, with effects confined to the shortest window (Table 2, cols. 1–2: −0.35, SE 0.06; −0.28, SE 0.09; Figure 2). This replicates, in a Colombian preschool sample, the acute-timing pattern found for school-age children and for preschoolers elsewhere. Quote the magnitudes as imprecise and probably at the high end of the literature.
- The social-emotional effect at 7 days (−0.34, SE 0.14, p ≈ .02; Table 2, col. 4) is real at conventional levels but would not survive a correction across five child domains, and its profile across windows is erratic. Cite it as suggestive, alongside the numeracy and literacy results, not on its own.
- The pedagogical-quality point estimates are negative at every pre-assessment window from 14 to 42 days (−0.37 to −0.60; Figure 3) and the three classroom placebos are null. This is a coherent pattern worth a follow-up study. It is the existence of a plausible signal that can be relied on, not its size.
- The design's mechanics as reported: 500 m radius, 7-day child and 14-day classroom windows, non-overlapping 90-day chronic-exposure control, one-week buffer exclusion, child or classroom fixed effects, SEs clustered by provider (pp.4–5; Table 2 note). These are stated clearly enough that a reader can judge what was estimated.
- The Data Availability Statement (p.6) is honest about why geocoded homicide and child data cannot be posted, and names the police data-use-agreement pathway.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Homicides reduce classroom pedagogical quality (d = .53 SD)" — borderline (p = .04), from about ten switching classrooms (count not reported), with within-unit changes in teacher education and learning materials that coincide with exposure (Table 1) and could produce a quality change without any change in how a given teacher teaches. Treat as a first estimate awaiting replication.
- "Effects detectable up to 6 weeks" — cumulative windows on different samples, not lags; the 21-day estimate is null (Figure 3). Read as "cumulative-window estimates remain negative through 42 days."
- "ds = –.14 SD to –.35 SD" on child outcomes — the lower bound is the non-significant motor estimate and the range omits executive functions, which is positive and significantly so at longer windows (Table 2, col. 5; Figure 2). Quote −0.28 to −0.35 for the two or three significant domains.
- "Particularly in classrooms with fewer baseline resources" and "protective factors" (abstract; pp.9–10) — rest entirely on unavailable Appendix Table 6, are called non-causal and hypothesis-generating by the authors (p.10), and involve the same variables that are imbalanced within units in Table 1.
- "Classroom quality may be a mechanism" (p.11) and "additional homicides cause worse between-child interactions" (p.7) — no mediation design; child and classroom effects are on different windows; the between-child-interaction item is not one of the two items the text names as significant.
- The Discussion's socio-emotional sentence ("up to 42 days," "–0.11 SD to –0.33 SD," p.10) — contradicted by Figure 2 (42-day estimate ≈ −0.07, not significant) and by the Results (p.7).
- "Future shocks … not consistently predictive" (p.7) — numeracy and executive functions are both significant at +14 days (Figure 2); the classroom +7 placebo (−0.25) has a CI wide enough to include the treatment effect.
- Any standard error quoted from the prose — the text gives 0.05 (numeracy) and 0.25 (pedagogical quality) where Table 2 prints 0.06 and 0.26; the second sits on the p = .05 boundary. Use the table.
- The positive executive-function effects (0.18–0.22 at 21, 28, 42 days) and the hypervigilance interpretation (p.10) — with 5 outcomes × 10 windows and no multiplicity adjustment, noise is the more economical reading.
- Balance and attendance claims — "substantially reduced" (p.4) is wrong for the center-level rows; "the running variable was not manipulated" (p.11) is regression-discontinuity language for a design with no running variable, and the underlying tests are in an unavailable appendix. Attendance selection after a homicide (p.11) is acknowledged, not handled.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Two wording corrections. Only the two 7-day cells flip sign (learning materials 0.51* → −0.63*; teacher higher education 0.24** → −0.47***); the 14-day cells keep their sign and grow (−0.60*** → −0.84***; −0.17* → −0.36***). And the p. 4 sentence names crime exposure and demographics, for which "substantially reduced" is true (the crime rows shrink from 1.24***, 0.77*** and 1.11*** to 0.07, 0.23* and −0.03, and the demographic rows go to about zero); it does not name learning materials or teacher education, so it is incomplete rather than wrong, which is how the Codex review read it. The within-unit imbalance on those two rows is real and the concern about the classroom estimate stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered table.

- The literature review as a secondary source — the Ang (2021), Abufhele & Laurito (2023), and "quasi-experimental studies overlook early childhood" (p.1, contradicted on p.2) characterizations should be checked before repeating; the Burdick-Will (2016) entry has no journal (it is Social Forces 95(1), 133–158 per the literature sub-review's check).
- Transportability to U.S. cities via citywide 2019 homicide rates (p.11) — hedged by the authors, and weak: exposure is a bundle of child, family, and teacher neighborhood exposure that the design cannot decompose.
