### Methods Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The design makes sense for the question. It compares the same child (or classroom) across two 2019 waves and uses the timing of nearby homicides relative to assessment dates, a tested approach in the community-violence literature. The paper's short-window child estimates (numeracy and literacy within 7 days) are its most credible results. The rating is driven by the paper's new contribution, the classroom-quality effect and the claim that classroom quality is a mechanism. That estimate is identified from very few switching units and a single-wave contrast. It sits right at p ≈ .05, and the paper's own Table 1 shows within-unit imbalance on teacher education and learning materials that the text describes as "substantially reduced." Several headline summaries (abstract effect range, "detectable up to 6 weeks," social-emotional persistence, falsification tests) also read the exhibits more favorably than the exhibits support.

**Strengths:**

- **Appropriate identification idea.** Within-child (first-difference) comparisons remove stable family, neighborhood and center confounders. The identifying assumption, that homicide timing near the ECEP is independent of other time-varying shocks, is stated explicitly, and the paper admits it cannot be tested with two waves (pp.5–6).
- **Strong measurement.** Children are assessed directly with IDELA, which has been validated in Colombia. Classroom process quality is observer-rated with IMCEIC. Homicide data come from geocoded police records, and homicide is the least under-reported violent crime (pp.4, 6).
- **The design is explicit about its checks.** It includes lead (+7/+14/+21) placebo windows, a buffer-week exclusion to sharpen the treated/untreated contrast, a chronic-exposure control that does not overlap the shock window, alternative radii, and a robbery comparison (pp.4–6).
- **Transparency about limitations.** The paper acknowledges small N, remaining imbalance, no pretrend test, attendance selection and non-random moderators (pp.10–11).
- **Child results match prior work.** The 7-day numeracy and literacy estimates (−0.35 and −0.28 SD; p.7, Table 2 cols. 1–2) agree in direction and rough size with prior short-window studies, including the lead author's own Colombian study.

**Weaknesses:**

- **Very little identifying variation, and it is not reported for the headline windows.** The only switcher count in the main text is 60 children for the 14-day window (p.5). The number of children switching at 7 days (the child headline) and the number of classrooms switching at 14 days (the classroom headline) are left to Appendix Table 5, which could not be checked. There are about 7 children per ECEP (298/43) and about 5.7 per classroom (298/52). By my inference, 60 child switchers correspond to roughly 8–10 ECEPs or classrooms. So each headline is probably identified from a single-digit-to-low-double-digit number of ECEP-wave shocks.
- **Clustered inference with 43 clusters and few treated clusters is likely too optimistic.** SEs are clustered by ECEP (p.5; p.7, Table 2). When only a handful of clusters carry the treatment variation, conventional cluster-robust SEs are known to over-reject. No wild-cluster bootstrap or randomization inference is reported in the main text. The numeracy SE of 0.06 (t ≈ 5.8) is surprisingly tight for this design.
- **Within-unit imbalance on the variables most likely to drive classroom quality (checkable).** In Table 1 (p.3), the FE-adjusted exposed-vs-unexposed differences stay large and significant for learning materials (−0.63* at 7 days; −0.84*** at 14 days) and teacher higher education (−0.47*** at 7 days; −0.36*** at 14 days). Dangerous conditions is also significant at 7 days (0.93*). For learning materials and teacher education, the FE-adjusted differences are *larger* in absolute size than the unadjusted ones (0.51 → −0.63; −0.60 → −0.84; 0.24 → −0.47; −0.17 → −0.36). That contradicts the p.4 statement that differences are "substantially reduced" once child FE are applied. With child FE, a nonzero FE-adjusted difference is only possible if the variable changes between waves. So either these center characteristics changed in step with exposure, which is a direct confounder for pedagogical quality, or the table has an error. The child models control only for chronic homicides and months between collections (p.7, Table 2 note). The classroom model adds "center-level structural quality indicators" (p.5), but these are not listed.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: the p. 4 sentence names crime and demographic rows, for which it is true.*

- **No wave/time fixed effect is shown, and how growth between waves is handled is unclear.** The equation on p.5 has no wave term. The paper does not say whether IDELA Z-scores are standardized within wave. The "months between collections" control appears constant within child: its FE-adjusted difference is blank in Table 1, p.3. If so, it is absorbed by the child FE and does not control for about 5.7 months of developmental growth between waves. If exposure is more common in one wave, β₁ could partly pick up that growth or differences between assessment rounds. A reader cannot resolve this from the text.
- **The classroom headline is fragile.** β = −0.53 with SE 0.26 (p.7, Table 2 col. 6), so t ≈ 2.04. It uses 102 observations, 52 classroom FE, clustering on 43 ECEPs, and weekday FE plus controls. It is the only significant classroom estimate at the specification the paper chose. The 21-day window is not significant (−0.47; p.9, Figure 3), and the number of activities is null (0.07; Table 2 col. 7).
- **Child and classroom windows do not line up, which weakens the mechanism claim.** Child effects are estimated at 7 days and classroom effects at 14 days (p.5; Table 2 note a). At −14 days, no child outcome is significant: numeracy ≈ −0.10, literacy ≈ 0.02, social-emotional ≈ −0.10, all n.s. (p.8, Figure 2). There is no 7-day classroom estimate. The Conclusions' claim that classroom quality "may be a mechanism" (p.11) comes from placing these side by side, not from a mediation design.
- **Cumulative windows are described as if they measured lagged effects.** Shocks are defined as homicides "within" X days (p.7, Table 2 note a), and the buffer rule excludes the week just before each window (pp.4–5). So the 42-day window includes the homicides from the first two weeks. It follows that "Effects detectable up to 6 weeks" (abstract) and "even if they occurred up to 6 weeks prior" (p.9) do not show that a homicide six weeks earlier lowers quality. Each window also uses a different sample because of the window-specific exclusion, so the estimates across windows are neither independent nor comparable.
- **The falsification tests are weaker than described.** By my reading of Figure 2 (p.8), 2 of the 15 child lead estimates are significant at p < .05: numeracy at +14 (≈ −0.11*, the same sign as the main effect) and executive function at +14 (≈ −0.17*). The text calls leads "not consistently predictive" (p.7). The Limitations section says they "generally" do not predict outcomes (p.11). Among classroom activity subcategories, leads are also significant for art (+7) and language (+14) (p.7, text; appendix figures not checkable).
- **Many tests, no adjustment.** There are 5 child outcomes × 7 windows + 3 leads, plus 2 classroom outcomes × 9, item-level, activity-by-subject, radius, robbery and heterogeneity analyses, with no multiplicity correction. The positive executive-function estimates at 3, 4 and 6 weeks (p.7; p.8, Figure 2) and the non-monotonic social-emotional pattern are what one would expect from noise in this many tests.
- **Attendance selection is admitted but not handled in the main text.** The analytic sample is children present in the assessment week at both waves (p.11), and 298 of 373 enrolled children remain (p.2). The p.11 claim that tests show "the running variable was not manipulated" uses regression-discontinuity language for a design with no running variable. The underlying tests are in Appendix A, which could not be checked.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Rely most on** the 7-day emergent numeracy (−0.35 SD) and emergent literacy/language (−0.28 SD) estimates (p.7, Table 2 cols. 1–2). They are the strongest, match prior literature, and would survive a Holm correction across the five child outcomes (my calculation). Treat the size as imprecise, since it probably comes from few ECEP-wave shocks. Also note the significant +14 lead for numeracy (p.8, Figure 2).
- **Treat the classroom pedagogical-quality effect (−0.53 SD per homicide at 14 days) as suggestive, not established.** It is borderline significant (p.7, Table 2 col. 6: t ≈ 2.0). It rests on few switching classrooms, and in the paper's own balance table the exposed waves have lower teacher education and fewer learning materials within the same unit (p.3, Table 1). The "first causal evidence" framing (pp.1, 9) is stronger than the evidence.
- **Read "effects up to 6 weeks" as "cumulative-window estimates up to 42 days remain negative."** They are not evidence that a homicide six weeks earlier still matters.
- **Do not treat classroom quality as a demonstrated mechanism** for the child effects. The windows do not overlap and no mediation analysis is done.
- **Discount the executive-function "positive effects"** (p.7; p.10) and the social-emotional "persistence" claims. The social-emotional pattern is non-monotonic: significant at 7, 21, 28 and 35 days, but ≈ −0.10 n.s. at 14 days and ≈ −0.07 n.s. at 42 days (p.8, Figure 2). The Results (p.7) and Discussion (p.10) also disagree on how far it extends.
- **The heterogeneity claims** in the abstract ("particularly in classrooms with fewer baseline resources") and the radius and robbery sensitivity analyses rest entirely on Appendix B (Appendix Table 6, Appendix Figures 8–9), which could not be checked. The authors themselves call the moderators non-randomly assigned (p.10). Treat them as hypothesis-generating.
- **Before building on the classroom finding**, check Appendix Table 5 (switcher counts by window), Appendix A (attendance/attrition), and whether a specification with a wave indicator and cluster-robust inference suited to few treated clusters gives the same answer.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and identifying assumption.* The paper uses a two-wave panel of 298 children in 52 classrooms across 43 publicly funded ECEPs in Bogotá and Cartagena (p.2). It regresses outcomes on the count of homicides within 500 m of the ECEP in a short window before assessment, with child (or classroom) fixed effects, a non-overlapping 90-day chronic-exposure control, and a buffer rule that drops observations exposed in the week just before the window (pp.4–5). With two observations per unit, this amounts to a first difference (p.5): β₁ is identified by children whose ECEP had a nearby homicide just before one assessment and not the other. The assumption is stated clearly (p.6): homicide timing is unrelated to other time-varying shocks. This is a reasonable design, and short-window timing comparisons like this have a good record. Its weakness is statistical power and how the variation is structured. Treatment is assigned at the ECEP-by-assessment-date level, children are clustered about 7 per ECEP, and homicides within 500 m in a 7- or 14-day window are rare. The effective number of independent "experiments" is therefore the number of ECEP-waves with a shock, not 298 or 557. The main text reports only the 14-day child switcher count (60 children; p.5). For the headline 7-day child window and the 14-day classroom window, readers must rely on Appendix Table 5, which I could not check.

*Sample accounting (checkable).* Table 2 reports 557 child-wave observations (p.7). With 298 children observed twice, the full panel would be 596. The odd total implies that the buffer exclusion (or missing data) removes individual child-waves rather than whole children, which leaves roughly 39 singleton children. With child FE, a singleton contributes nothing to β₁ but still counts toward N and inflates R². This does not bias β₁, but "N = 557" (and the R² of .75–.86) overstates the information in the estimate. The classroom models use 102 of 104 possible classroom-waves (p.7, Table 2 cols. 6–7). The text does not explain which two are dropped.

*Balance and confounding.* Table 1 (p.3) is where readers should look most carefully. Before FE, exposed and unexposed observations differ a great deal in chronic crime (homicides, assaults and robberies all about +0.8 to +1.2 SD, p < .001). That is expected, because violent areas have more homicides in any window. The FE-adjusted chronic-homicide gap shrinks to 0.07/0.11 SD, which is reassuring. Chronic assaults do not shrink as much (0.23*, 0.18*), and assaults are not controlled. The center-level rows are more worrying. Time-invariant variables correctly show FE-adjusted differences of exactly 0.00 (female, baseline age, center-based care), which confirms the FE adjustment is working as described. Learning materials, teacher higher education and (at 7 days) dangerous conditions, however, show large and significant FE-adjusted differences, larger than the unadjusted ones for the first two. For these to be nonzero within a child, they must have been re-measured and changed between waves, most plausibly through teacher turnover or materials changes at specific ECEPs. When the treatment varies in only a handful of ECEP-waves, any coincidental ECEP-wave change like a new, less-credentialed teacher is confounded with exposure. This is especially serious for pedagogical quality, which is measured through the teacher's behavior. It is possible that these characteristics are among the "center-level structural quality indicators" included in the classroom model (p.5), but they are not listed. In the child models, they are not controlled (p.7, Table 2 note). A reader should also consider the opposite reading: violence might cause teacher turnover, which prior work has documented. In that case these variables are mediators, and controlling for them would be inappropriate. Either way, the p.4 sentence that imbalances are "substantially reduced" does not describe these rows accurately. The Limitations sentence that "some imbalance in observables remains" (p.11) is closer to the truth.

Two smaller Table 1 oddities are worth noting (SUSPECTED, low stakes). First, the 7-day "Unexposed" means and SDs for caregiver higher education (0.36/0.48), mother's age (28.17/6.21) and household adults (3.18/1.86) are identical to the full-baseline-sample values. That is possible, but it may be a copying artifact. Second, the note says "Units are expressed in standard deviations," yet most rows are clearly in raw units (e.g., age 45.35 months, female 0.45).

*Specification details.* Several things a reader would want are not visible in the main text. (i) Time/wave fixed effects: the p.5 equation has none, and whether outcomes are standardized within wave is not stated. With pooled standardization and a months-between control that is constant within child (Table 1 shows a blank FE-adjusted difference for it), nothing would absorb the May-to-November growth. β₁ would then be biased by growth whenever exposure is unevenly split across waves. (ii) Weekday FE: the Table 2 note and the Figure 2–4 notes say assessment-weekday FE are included. The equation on p.5 leaves them out, although the p.5 text mentions controlling for "the assessment day." This is in substance consistent, just incompletely written out (checkable). For classrooms, the paper says the observation date is known only to the week (p.5), yet the figure notes list "assessment weekday" FE for classroom models (p.9, Figures 3–4). (iii) Chronic window for classrooms: the Table 2 note defines chronic exposure as days 8–97, which fits the 7-day child model. For the 14-day classroom model it should be 15–104 days. The note describes only the child version.

*Inference.* Clustering on ECEP is the right level given how treatment is assigned, but 43 clusters with few treated clusters is exactly the setting where standard cluster-robust SEs are too small. Homicides can also fall within 500 m of more than one ECEP (the overlapping rings in Figure 1, p.5, are illustrative), so one event can "treat" several clusters. ECEP-level clustering does not capture that dependence. The classroom estimate is t ≈ 2.04 on roughly 40 residual degrees of freedom (my estimate: 102 observations minus 52 FE minus controls and weekday dummies). A modest correction would push it past .05. Under a Holm correction across the two classroom outcomes it already fails (.04 × 2 = .08; my calculation). Among the 7-day child outcomes, a Holm correction across five domains keeps numeracy and literacy (p ≈ .001 and ≈ .003 from Table 2's t-ratios) but drops social-emotional (.02 × 3 = .06). All three calculations are mine.

*Time windows, leads, and persistence claims.* The windows are cumulative ("within" X days; p.7, Table 2 note), and each is estimated on a different sample because of the window-specific buffer exclusion (pp.4–5). The resulting profiles are therefore not event-study lag coefficients. The social-emotional profile shows the problem. It is ≈ −0.34* at 7 days, ≈ −0.10 n.s. at 14 days, ≈ −0.28* to −0.33** at 21–35 days, and ≈ −0.07 to −0.12 n.s. at 42–49 days (p.8, Figure 2). If the 7-day effect were real and cumulative windows included it, the 14-day estimate should not fall to near zero. The pattern looks like a few influential ECEP-waves moving in and out of the treated and excluded groups. The text also describes this profile two different ways: "–0.28 SD to –0.34 SD … within 35 days … null for longer windows" (p.7) versus "up to 42 days … –0.11 SD to –0.33 SD" (p.10). The executive-function estimates are positive and significant at 21, 28 and 42 days (≈ 0.18–0.22; p.8, Figure 2; text on p.7 gives 0.18–0.20). The paper considers a hyper-vigilance story and then partly rejects it (p.10). The more economical reading is noise across dozens of tests. For pedagogical quality (p.9, Figure 3), the pre-period estimates are −0.53* (14 days), −0.47 n.s. (21), −0.57*** (28), −0.60*** (35), −0.37* (42) and −0.15 n.s. (49). The leads are −0.25, −0.03 and 0.09, all n.s. This profile is more consistent than the child profiles, which is modestly reassuring. The −0.25 at +7 is not trivial, however, and the CI is wide. For the leads overall, 2 of 15 child lead coefficients are significant (numeracy +14 and executive function +14; p.8, Figure 2), about 13% against 5% expected by chance. That is not damning, but it is weaker than "bolstering our claims of causality" (p.7).

*Attendance and sample selection.* Parents may keep children home after a nearby homicide, and assessment day within the week may shift (p.11). If lower-functioning or more-affected children are the ones who stay home, the estimates are biased toward zero. If the reverse is true, they are biased away from zero. The analytic sample also conditions on assessment at both waves (298/373, p.2). The paper's reassurance, "the running variable was not manipulated" (p.11), is regression-discontinuity language that does not fit this design, and the tests themselves are in Appendix A, which I could not check.

*Headline summaries vs. exhibits (checkable).* The abstract says CVE "lowers child developmental performance … (ds = –.14 SD to –.35 SD)." That range is the four negative 7-day point estimates in Table 2 (p.7). Its lower end is motor (−0.14, SE 0.13), which the text itself calls not different from zero (p.6), and it leaves out executive function (+0.12). A fairer summary is two or three significant domains at −0.28 to −0.35. The abstract's "effects detectable up to 6 weeks" matches Figure 3's significant −42 estimate (−0.37*). Given cumulative windows and the n.s. 21-day estimate, it should not be read as a six-week lag. The text also differs from Table 2 in two places: numeracy SE is 0.05 in the text (p.6) but 0.06 in Table 2 col. 1 (p.7), and pedagogical-quality SE is 0.25 in the text (p.7) but 0.26 in Table 2 col. 6. The second discrepancy matters a little, because it sits on the p = .05 boundary. Finally, the robbery comparison is described inconsistently: "property crimes" (p.6), "nonlethal robberies … effects are primarily driven by violent crimes" (p.9), "a negative effect related to robberies … statistically insignificant for all other child-level outcomes" (p.10, which implies at least one significant robbery effect), and "outcomes are not affected by nonviolent crimes" (p.11). The underlying Appendix Figure 9 could not be checked.

*External validity.* The sample is low-income children in publicly funded ECEPs in two high-violence Colombian cities, observed in one year (p.2; p.11). The authors correctly note that ECEP-proximity exposure cannot be separated from home or teacher exposure (pp.10–11). Effects are reported per additional homicide, and since most exposed units probably see one event, the estimate should not be extrapolated linearly to higher counts.

*Bottom line.* The paper uses a sensible design to replicate a short-lived drop in young children's numeracy and literacy after nearby homicides, and that finding deserves moderate weight. Its new claims are that homicides lower observed classroom process quality, that this lasts up to six weeks, and that it is a channel for child effects. These rest on a borderline estimate from few switching classrooms, with within-unit imbalance in teacher and materials characteristics visible in the paper's own Table 1, and on a reading of cumulative windows as lags. They should be treated as a promising hypothesis, not an established result.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper covers the core recent literature on acute community-violence exposure (CVE) and child test performance, and its narrow headline, that this is the first causal estimate of homicides' effect on *observed* early-childhood classroom process quality, appears to hold as far as I know. Around that headline, though, the scholarly positioning is thin and sometimes inaccurate. The paper says prior work offers "little evidence" on mechanisms, yet existing studies already document school-functioning channels (teacher absence and turnover, school climate). Several citations are described more loosely than their sources support. The paper does not reconcile its effect sizes, or its positive executive-function estimates, with the closest comparable studies, including the lead author's own 2024 paper. Readers should cite this paper for the classroom-quality estimate and turn to its predecessors for the broader picture.

**Strengths:**

- Covers the core acute-exposure literature in economics, sociology and developmental psychology: Sharkey et al. (2012), McCoy et al. (2015, 2024), Abufhele & Laurito (2023), Chang & Padilla-Romo (2023), Monteiro & Rocha (2017), Koppensteiner & Menezes (2021), Burdick-Will (2013, 2016) and Schwartz et al. (2022) (pp.1–2, 4, 6; references pp.11–13). It draws on Latin American evidence rather than only U.S. studies.
- The narrow novelty claim, a causal estimate of recent homicides' effect on *observation-rated* ECE classroom process quality (pp.1, 9, 11), is to my knowledge accurate. I know of no earlier quasi-experimental study that uses an observed process-quality instrument as the outcome.
- The paper gives a reasonable, cited rationale for using homicides as the exposure measure (lower underreporting, salience; Lauritsen et al., 2016; Range & Thompson, 1987; p.4). Following McCoy et al. (2015), it excludes children exposed in the week before each window, and it uses future homicides as a placebo, as the design literature does (pp.4–6).
- It correctly notes that Monteiro & Rocha (2017) documented teacher-side disruption (p.2). CONFIRMED-BY-ME online: that paper reports that gunfights are associated with higher teacher absenteeism, principal turnover and temporary school closings. The paper's wording, "teacher absences and turnover", is broadly accurate, though the turnover Monteiro & Rocha report is *principal* turnover.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The mechanisms gap is oversold.** The Discussion says "there is little evidence on the nature of the potential mechanisms" (p.9), and the Introduction says it "remains unclear" whether violence-related disruptions affect teaching (p.2). Economics already has causal evidence on school-functioning channels: Monteiro & Rocha (2017; cited) and Jarillo, Magaloni, Franco & Robles (2016, *International Journal of Educational Development*; not cited). CONFIRMED-BY-ME online: Jarillo et al. report instructional-time losses from higher teacher absenteeism and turnover, plus student absenteeism, under Mexican drug violence. Laurito, Lacoe, Schwartz, Sharkey & Ellen (2019, *RSF*; not cited) show that effects of neighborhood violent crime on test scores are larger in schools perceived as less safe or weaker in community. CONFIRMED-BY-ME online. The defensible claim is narrower: the first causal estimate on *observed ECE process quality*. The broader claim, that school-level mechanisms were previously unexamined, is not defensible.
- **The paper contradicts itself on early childhood.** Page 1 says prior quasi-experimental studies "typically focus on school-age children … and overlook the early childhood stage." Page 2 then cites three quasi-experimental preschool studies (Abufhele & Laurito, 2023; McCoy et al., 2024; Sharkey et al., 2012), and pp.4–5 cite a fourth (McCoy et al., 2015). CONFIRMED-BY-ME from the text. The real gap is about ECE *settings and classroom processes*, not about the age group.
- **Ang (2021) is mischaracterized (p.10).** The text says Ang's "sensitivity model … suggests that the effects of exposure to homicides are detectable if they occur within 0.5 miles (804 m) of children's homes." Ang's paper, titled "The effects of police violence on inner-city students" in the reference list (p.12), studies *police killings* in Los Angeles, not homicides in general. CONFIRMED-BY-ME from the reference-list title; the Los Angeles/police-killings content is from my own knowledge of the paper. Using it to say the present paper's 800–850 m decay "aligns very closely" compares different kinds of events, different anchors (the home versus the ECEP), and different ages and outcomes.
- **Abufhele & Laurito (2023) is described at the wrong spatial scale (p.2).** The paper groups it with studies showing that "recent homicides near the home" reduce outcomes. CONFIRMED-BY-ME online (Europe PMC abstract): Abufhele & Laurito measure homicides at the *municipality* level in the month before a PPVT assessment. They compare Chilean children in the same municipality assessed before versus after the homicides and find effects of 0.18–0.41 SD. The finding is relevant, but it is not evidence about proximity to the home. The citation year is also inconsistent: the article appeared online in 2023 but is cited with the 2024 volume and issue, 95(3), 800–816 (p.12).
- **The paper does not say how it relates to Cristancho et al. (2024).** The lead author's own *Child Development* paper is cited only inside citation strings (pp.1, 4) and its findings are never described. CONFIRMED-BY-ME from the text. CONFIRMED-BY-ME online (Europe PMC abstract): that paper finds that homicides within 7 days and 500 m of a school reduce 5th- and 9th-grade test scores by 0.10 SD, with effects fading as the window widens. The present paper's main specification (7 days, 500 m; Table 2, p.7) is identical, but it never says the specification was carried over. That omission matters, because a specification set in advance by prior work reduces forking-paths concerns and would count in the paper's favor.
  - A correction to a common assumption: this is **not** the same cities or data year. A ResearchGate figure caption and a search-engine summary indicate that the 2024 paper used Cali and Medellín SABER tests from 2012. The present paper uses Bogotá and Cartagena in 2019 (p.2). I have partial online confirmation: the abstract says only "two Colombian cities", and I could not open the full text.
  - The child-level estimates here (−0.28 to −0.35 SD per homicide for literacy and numeracy; Table 2, p.7) are roughly three times the 2024 estimate from the same specification. The paper does not discuss this gap.
- **The paper does not engage conflicting evidence.**
  - *Executive functions.* On p.2 the paper cites Sharkey et al. (2012) and McCoy et al. (2024) for reduced attention, impulse control and regulation. It then reports *positive* effects on executive functions of 0.18–0.20 SD at 3-, 4- and 6-week windows (pp.7, 10; Figure 2, p.8). It discusses this finding (p.10) without saying that it runs against the regulatory findings it cited. CONFIRMED-BY-ME online: McCoy et al. (2024) report *lower* effortful control after recent homicides.
  - *Magnitudes.* McCoy et al. (2024) find d = .05–.20 in a São Paulo sample of 3,241 three-year-olds (CONFIRMED-BY-ME online). The present paper's N is 298 (p.10). Yet p.10 says children here are affected "similarly to what has been documented in other contexts." Small samples with larger-than-typical estimates are a known pattern that readers should weigh.
- **Some supporting citations do not support their claims.** For the claim that young children "may be more sensitive to changes in the behavior of caregivers and teachers than to violent incidents themselves" (p.2), the paper cites Finkelhor et al. (2015). That is a prevalence survey (title on p.12; CONFIRMED-BY-ME from the reference list). It also cites Von Suchodoletz et al. (2023), a meta-analysis of associations between ECE quality and child outcomes (title on p.13). Neither tests the claim. Leventhal (2018), a short *Child Development Perspectives* piece on developmental timing in neighborhood effects (p.12), is cited for what quasi-experimental CVE studies "typically focus on" (p.1). SUSPECTED weak fit; I have not read it in full.
- **The Burdick-Will (2016) reference is incomplete (p.11).** The entry ends with "Neighborhood Violence and Academic Growth." and gives no journal. CONFIRMED-BY-ME online: the article is *Social Forces*, 95(1), 133–158 (2016), DOI 10.1093/sf/sow041. It is a study of *chronic, early* neighborhood violence and test-score growth. That fits p.6's use of it to compare violent and property crime, but it is not an acute-timing study.
- **Design antecedents are missing.** The paper does not cite the foundational day-level design, Sharkey (2010, *PNAS*): children in the same neighborhood are assessed just before or just after a local homicide. It also omits Sharkey, Schwartz, Ellen & Lacoe (2014, *Sociological Science*); Gershenson & Tekin (2018, *Education Finance and Policy*, on the Beltway sniper attacks); Caudillo & Torche (2014, *Sociology of Education*, on Mexico); and Michaelsen & Salardi (2020, *Journal of Development Economics*; CONFIRMED-BY-ME online). Michaelsen & Salardi find the largest effects from homicides near schools in the week before tests. The others I list from my own knowledge.
  - The paper does not explain how its two-wave within-child first-differences design (p.5), identified by about 60 switchers in the 14-day window (p.5), relates to these cross-sectional timing designs, or why it departs from them.
  - It borrows the language of that literature: p.11 says tests confirmed "the running variable was not manipulated". But no regression-discontinuity or running-variable design is described in the Methods. Readers should not assume the design was benchmarked against event-study or discontinuity approaches.
- **No classroom-observation measurement literature.** The headline is a 0.53 SD effect (Table 2, p.7; SE 0.26 in the table, 0.25 in the text) on a 9-item scale with α = .72 (p.4). Each classroom is observed once per wave, during the assessment week (p.5), for 102 classroom-wave observations (Table 2, p.7). The main text says nothing about rater training, interrater agreement, how raters were assigned across waves, or observation length. CONFIRMED-BY-ME: text search finds no mention.
  - Rater drift across data-collection periods is documented and can be large: Casabianca, Lockwood & McCaffrey (2015, *Educational and Psychological Measurement*) found it persisted over two years of CLASS-S scoring (CONFIRMED-BY-ME online). With a May and a November wave, drift is a live concern.
  - Occasion-level variance and short observation windows are also documented (Mashburn et al., 2014; Hill, Charalambous & Kraft, 2012; Curby et al., 2011; from my own knowledge). None of this literature is cited.
- **The teacher-stress literature is missing.** The paper interprets its results as disruption to teachers' planning and emotional well-being (p.10), but it cites no work linking teacher stressors to classroom climate. Examples include Jennings & Greenberg's (2009) prosocial-classroom model (from my own knowledge) and Li-Grining, Raver et al. (2010, *Early Education and Development*), who found mixed evidence linking Head Start teachers' psychosocial stressors to classroom climate and behavior management (CONFIRMED-BY-ME online). No qualitative work on teaching in violent neighborhoods is engaged.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **What to cite this paper for.** Cite it for a small-sample causal estimate linking recent nearby homicides to lower *observed* pedagogical quality in Colombian public ECE classrooms. Do not cite it for the claim that school or teacher mechanisms were previously unstudied; for that, cite Monteiro & Rocha (2017), Jarillo et al. (2016) and Laurito et al. (2019).
- **Read it alongside Cristancho et al. (2024, *Child Development*).** Same lead author, same 7-day/500 m specification, but school-age children in, as I understand it, different cities (Cali and Medellín, 2012). That paper's 0.10 SD estimate is a more precise benchmark than the 0.28–0.35 SD child-level estimates here (Table 2, p.7).
- **For the preschool child-outcome evidence, lean on the larger studies.** McCoy et al. (2024; N = 3,241; d = .05–.20) and Abufhele & Laurito (2023; municipality-level exposure) are the anchors. Treat this paper's child-level estimates as noisy corroboration.
- **Check before repeating:**
  - the p.10 use of Ang (2021), which is about police killings rather than homicides in general;
  - the p.2 description of Abufhele & Laurito as "near the home" (their exposure is municipality-wide);
  - the p.1 claim that quasi-experimental studies overlook early childhood;
  - the Burdick-Will (2016) reference, whose correct source is *Social Forces* 95(1), 133–158.
- **For design context, read Sharkey (2010, *PNAS*) and Michaelsen & Salardi (2020).** They show how day-level timing designs work and what their identifying comparisons are. A useful overview of the field is Sharkey (2018, *Annual Review of Criminology*, "The long reach of violence"; cited from my own knowledge).
- **To judge the 0.53 SD quality effect, read Casabianca et al. (2015) on rater drift and Hill, Charalambous & Kraft (2012) on observation reliability.** For scale, Egert, Fukkink & Eckhardt (2018, *Review of Educational Research*) estimate that in-service professional development raises ECE quality ratings by about 0.68 SD (CONFIRMED-BY-ME online). A single nearby homicide lowering observed quality by nearly that much is a strong claim that deserves corroboration. Kraft (2020, *Educational Researcher*) offers general guidance on effect-size benchmarks.
- **Know that the outcome instrument is the authors' own.** IMCEIC was developed by a team that includes two of the authors (Maldonado-Carreño et al., 2022). The paper does not say whether the 2019 two-city sample overlaps with the national IMCEIC study, and the item list (Appendix Table 2) is in the online supplement, which I could not check.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Where the paper sits.* This is a short Feature Article with about 40 references, so a complete survey is not expected. But the positioning determines how readers will use the paper, and here the framing runs ahead of the literature. The contribution is real and narrow. It is the first causal estimate, to my knowledge, of an effect of nearby homicides on *observation-rated* process quality in ECE classrooms, plus a replication of acute child-level effects in a Colombian preschool sample. The paper instead describes itself as opening the question of *mechanisms* in general (p.9: "little evidence on the nature of the potential mechanisms"; p.11: "a major finding in this literature that has included limited process measures"). Economists have studied school-functioning channels for about a decade.

- Monteiro & Rocha (2017) show that Rio gang battles raise teacher absenteeism and principal turnover and close schools temporarily.
- Jarillo et al. (2016) show instructional-time losses from teacher absenteeism and turnover under Mexican drug violence.
- Laurito et al. (2019) show that school safety climate moderates the effect of neighborhood violence on test scores in New York City.

These studies measure school functioning through administrative or survey data, not structured classroom observation. So "first on observed process quality" survives. "First on mechanisms" does not. Readers who repeat the broader claim will misstate the literature.

*The authors' own prior work.* The most important piece of context is left almost unused. Cristancho et al. (2024) is an earlier paper by the same lead author and two of the same co-authors (Bailey, Duncan) plus Norza. It uses a 7-day window and a 500 m radius around schools, finds 0.10 SD effects on school-age test scores that fade as the window widens, and appears to use different cities and years (Cali and Medellín, 2012) from the present study (Bogotá and Cartagena, 2019). The present paper reuses that exact specification for its headline child results (Table 2, p.7; Table 1 note, p.3: "Following the main specification…"). It does not say the specification was set by prior work, and it does not compare magnitudes. This undersells one strength, since a specification inherited from earlier work is less vulnerable to specification search. It also hides one tension: child effects roughly three times larger in a sample about one-sixteenth the size (N = 298, p.10, versus N = 4,729 in the 2024 abstract). Readers should hold both in mind.

*Characterization accuracy.* Most citations are described acceptably, but several are not reliable enough to repeat. The Ang (2021) mismatch on p.10 is the clearest. Ang studies police killings, and she measures distance from students' residences, not from schools or ECEPs. So the "very close" agreement with this paper's 800–850 m decay compares different events and different anchors. The description of Abufhele & Laurito as "near the home" (p.2) mixes up spatial scales: their exposure is municipality-level. On p.1, the list of studies showing effects "especially when violent incidents occur days before an assessment" includes Burdick-Will (2013; school violent-crime rates), Schwartz et al. (2022; chronic exposure) and Molano et al. (2018; mental health). None of these is an acute-timing test-score study. The supporting citations for the claim that young children are more sensitive to caregivers' behavior than to violence itself (p.2) do not test that claim. None of these problems changes the paper's own estimates, but readers should not use its literature review as a secondary source.

*Conflicting evidence.* The paper reports two findings that cut against the literature it cites, and it discusses neither as a conflict.

1. Positive executive-function effects at longer windows (pp.7, 10). Sharkey et al. (2012) and McCoy et al. (2024) find reduced attention, impulse control or effortful control after recent homicides. The paper's post hoc hypervigilance explanation (p.10) is offered and then partly withdrawn in the same paragraph. A reader would conclude the executive-function result is more likely noise than a new phenomenon.
2. Effect magnitudes. The best-powered comparable preschool study, McCoy et al. (2024), finds d = .05–.20. The present estimates are at or above the top of that range for every significant child outcome, and 0.53 SD for classroom quality.

Large acute effects do have precedent: from my own knowledge, Sharkey (2010) reported effects of about half an SD for Black children in Chicago whose block group had a homicide in the week before assessment. The fuller evidence base still suggests that typical acute effects on preschoolers are small to moderate, and that small samples tend to produce larger estimates.

*Adjacent literatures that change the reading.* Two bodies of work that bear directly on the headline outcome are absent.

- **Classroom-observation measurement.** Each classroom is observed once per wave on a 9-item scale with α = .72 (p.4). The effect is identified from changes between a May and a November observation. Rater drift and severity differences (Casabianca et al., 2015) and occasion-level variance (Hill, Charalambous & Kraft, 2012; Mashburn et al., 2014) could produce, or hide, within-classroom changes of the size reported, unless raters were balanced across exposure status and waves. The main text is silent on this.
- **Teacher stress and classroom climate.** This literature, from Jennings & Greenberg's (2009) model to Li-Grining, Raver et al.'s (2010) Head Start findings, would give the teacher-disruption interpretation on p.10 a theoretical basis. It would also caution that the correlational links between stressors and observed climate are mixed.

Benchmarking would help as well. The paper cites Von Suchodoletz et al. (2023) but does not use it to translate a 0.53 SD quality drop into expected child impacts. It also does not note that intensive professional development raises ECE quality ratings by about 0.68 SD on average (Egert et al., 2018), which makes the scale of the claim clear.

*Design positioning.* The design literature in economics and sociology mostly uses cross-sectional variation in assessment timing: the same neighborhood, before versus after a homicide, around fixed or varying test dates (Sharkey, 2010; Chang & Padilla-Romo, 2023; Michaelsen & Salardi, 2020; Abufhele & Laurito, 2023; McCoy et al., 2024; Cristancho et al., 2024). The present paper instead uses two-wave within-child first differences (p.5). Each approach has tradeoffs, and the paper states several limitations itself (no pre-trends, p.11). It never explains why it chose this design over the standard one or what that choice implies for comparing estimates. The mention of a "running variable" (p.11) suggests the analysis inherits concepts from a discontinuity framing that is not described in the Methods. Readers comparing this estimate with the timing-design literature should treat the designs as different, not as replications.

*What could not be checked.* The online supplement (Appendices A–B, Appendix Tables 2–6, Appendix Figures 2–9) was unavailable to me. It may contain further literature engagement, the IMCEIC item list, and details on observation procedures that bear on the measurement points above. Online, I verified the existence and content of Abufhele & Laurito, McCoy et al. (2024), Cristancho et al. (2024; abstract only), Maldonado-Carreño et al. (2022; abstract only), Burdick-Will (2016), Monteiro & Rocha (2017), Jarillo et al. (2016), Laurito et al. (2019), Li-Grining et al. (2010), Michaelsen & Salardi (2020), Casabianca et al. (2015) and Egert et al. (2018). Other characterizations, including Ang (2021), Sharkey (2010), Sharkey et al. (2014), Gershenson & Tekin (2018), Caudillo & Torche (2014), Hill et al. (2012), Mashburn et al. (2014), Curby et al. (2011), Jennings & Greenberg (2009), Sharkey (2018) and Kraft (2020), come from my own knowledge. The cities in Cristancho et al. (2024) are supported only by a figure caption and a search-engine summary, not by the full text.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper is short, conventionally organized, and its headline exhibit (Table 2) is clean and easy to read. The prose, though, repeatedly describes the evidence differently from what the exhibits show. The abstract's child-effect range includes a null estimate and leaves out a positive one. The Results and Discussion give different versions of the social-emotional time pattern, and the Discussion's version conflicts with Figure 2. The balance narrative says Table 1's differences shrink under fixed effects, but for several rows they grow. Robbery results are described in contradictory terms. A reader should treat the figures and Table 2 as the record and check every number in the prose against them before quoting it.

**Strengths:**

- The format is compact and conventional (Introduction, Method, Results, Sensitivity, Discussion, Limitations, Conclusions). The research questions (a)–(d) and the hypotheses are stated explicitly on p.2, so readers can tell what the paper set out to test.
- Table 2 (p.7) is a clean, self-contained headline exhibit. It has seven columns with a clear child/classroom split, coefficients with SEs and stars, R², N, and a footnote that states the exposure window for each block (7 days for child outcomes, 14 days for classroom outcomes).
- Figures 2–4 (pp.8–9) show every time window with 95% CIs. They include the post-assessment falsification windows (+7/+14/+21) in the same panel, so readers can compare "pre" and "placebo" estimates directly. Figures 3 and 4 label each point estimate numerically, which lets readers check the prose.
- The five panels of Figure 2 share one y-axis scale (−.5 to .5), so effect sizes can be compared across child domains.
- The identifying assumption is stated plainly (p.6), and so is the first-differences equivalence of the two-wave FE design (p.5). The Limitations section says openly that pretrends cannot be tested with two waves (p.11).
- The Figure 1 map (p.5) is honest and checkable. The 500 m rings match the scale bar (about 1 km across), and the legend matches the caption.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The abstract's child-effect range is misleading.** It gives "ds = –.14 SD to –.35 SD" (p.1). The –.14 is the non-significant motor estimate (p.7, Table 2, col. 3; p = .27 per p.6), and the positive executive-function estimate (+0.12, col. 5) is left out. Only three of the five child domains are significant at 7 days. The abstract also leaves out the positive executive-function effects at 3, 4, and 6 weeks (Figure 2), which run against the hypothesis. Its "particularly in classrooms with fewer baseline resources" rests entirely on Appendix Table 6, which has no numbers in the main text (p.9).
- **The social-emotional persistence claim is told two ways, and neither fully matches Figure 2.** Results (pp.6–7) say effects of "–0.28 SD to –0.34 SD" persist within 35 days and "only become null for longer windows." In Figure 2 (p.8), though, the 14-day estimate is about –0.10 with a CI crossing zero. The Discussion (p.10) extends the claim to a "long-lived effect ... up to 42 days ... ranging from –0.11 SD to –0.33 SD." In Figure 2 the 42-day estimate is about –0.07 and not significant.
- **The Discussion contradicts itself on child-effect persistence.** One paragraph on p.10 claims long-lived social-emotional effects. The next says "we do not observe statistically significant child-level effects for more distant exposures." Figure 2 shows significant social-emotional estimates at 21, 28, and 35 days, and significant executive-function estimates at 21, 28, and 42 days.
- **The balance narrative runs against Table 1.** The text says between-group differences "are substantially reduced when adjusting for within-child variation" (p.4). In Table 1 (p.3), the FE-adjusted differences for learning materials and teacher education are larger in magnitude than the unadjusted ones, change sign, and stay significant, in both the 7-day and 14-day samples. These are the same center characteristics the Discussion later calls "protective factors" (p.10).

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: only the 7-day cells flip sign, and the p. 4 sentence names other rows.*

- **The robbery placebo is described inconsistently.** It is called "property crimes" (p.6), "nonlethal robberies" (p.9), "robberies (excluding those involving assaults and homicides)" with "a negative effect" on an unnamed outcome (p.10), and "nonviolent crimes" with no effect (p.11). A reader cannot tell what was estimated or what it showed, and Appendix Figure 9 is not available.
- **Terminology and specification drift.** The Limitations refer to a "running variable" that was "not manipulated" (p.11), but this is a two-wave FE design with no running variable. Weekday controls appear in the Table 2 note ("weekday of the assessment fixed effects") and in the Figure 2–4 notes, but not in the Fixed-effects subsection (p.5). The time windows are listed as 7–42 days (p.4) but analyzed as 1–7 weeks, including –49 (p.5; Figs. 2–4). Figure 4 plots the "overall number of activities" but the text calls it "overall quality of activities" (p.7).
- **Much of the load-bearing material is in a supplement with no numbers in the main text.** This covers attrition (Appendix A), exposure and switcher counts (Appendix Tables 4–5), heterogeneity (Appendix Table 6), item-level effects (Appendix Figure 3), activity subtypes (Appendix Figures 4–7), radius sensitivity (Appendix Figure 8), and robberies (Appendix Figure 9). The main-text "Sensitivity Analyses" section is a single paragraph with no estimates. The Discussion then brings in new quantitative claims (radii "300 m and 600 m," "800 m and 850 m," p.10) that appear nowhere in Results. I did not have access to the supplement and cannot assess it.
- **The headline analytic N is not reconciled.** 298 children × 2 waves = 596, but Table 2 reports N = 557. 52 classrooms × 2 = 104, but Table 2 reports 102. The text never gives the arithmetic. The only switcher count given (60 children, p.5) refers to a 2-week window, not the 7-day window behind the child headline estimates.
- **Figure 2 is hard to read in print.** It is rotated 90° on p.8, has no numeric point labels (unlike Figures 3–4), and uses very small significance stars. The bold "–7\*" / "–14\*" tick labels mark the main specification, but they use the same asterisk as the significance legend and are not explained anywhere. The child figure (±.5 axis) and the classroom figures (–1 to 1.5 axis) are on different scales.
- **Production errors that survived to print:** "ECECs" (p.5), "800 ms" (p.9), "ordinary leas squares" (Figure 2 note, p.8), "Emerging" vs. "Emergent" and "Socioemotional" vs. "Social-Emotional" across exhibits, and a Table 2 title that says "on Children's Outcomes" over two classroom columns. The Burdick-Will (2016) reference has no journal, volume, pages, or DOI (p.12). The Fowler et al. (2009) entry has spelling errors ("childen," "Psycopathology").

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Read these closely:** Table 2 (p.7), Figure 2 (p.8; rotate the page), and Figure 3 (p.9). Together they are the paper's evidence. Take the per-window numbers from the figures, not the prose.
- **Headline estimates, stated correctly:** the effects are per additional homicide within 500 m. For children (7-day window): numeracy –0.35 (SE 0.06), literacy –0.28 (0.09), and social-emotional –0.34 (0.14) are significant; motor –0.14 (0.13) and executive functions +0.12 (0.13) are not (p.7, Table 2). For pedagogical quality (14-day window): –0.53 (SE 0.26), p ≈ .04, with a 95% CI running from about –1.04 to about 0 (Figure 3). The classroom effect is imprecisely estimated from 102 classroom-waves.
- **Use Table 2's SEs, not the prose.** The text gives 0.05 for numeracy and 0.25 for pedagogical quality.
- **Pedagogical quality "up to 6 weeks":** Figure 3 shows significance at 14, 28, 35, and 42 days, but **not** at 21 days (–0.47, CI crossing zero) or 49 days. The "–0.37 to –0.60" range (pp.7, 9) is correct as a range of point estimates, but it includes the non-significant 21-day estimate.
- **Do not quote the Discussion's social-emotional sentence** ("up to 42 days," "–0.11 to –0.33," p.10). Figure 2 shows significant estimates at 7, 21, 28, and 35 days only. The 14-day and 42-day estimates are null.
- **Placebo windows:** the prose says future homicides are "not consistently predictive" (p.7). Figure 2 shows 2 of the 15 child-level placebo coefficients are significant: numeracy +14 (≈ –0.11) and executive functions +14 (≈ –0.16). Readers should weigh this themselves.
- **Balance:** read Table 1's FE-adjusted columns directly, especially the learning-materials and teacher-education rows (p.3). Do not rely on the p.4 summary.
- **Skim:** the Introduction and the first two Discussion paragraphs, which largely repeat each other ("Addressing this gap ..." / "We address this gap ...," p.9). Also skim the intervention and generalizability paragraphs placed under Limitations (p.11).
- **Treat as unverifiable from the article alone:** the heterogeneity claims (abstract; p.9; p.10), the radius-sensitivity claims (pp.9–10), the robbery placebo, the item-level "drivers" of the quality effect (pp.7, 9), and the activity-subtype shifts. All of them rest on supplementary exhibits whose numbers are not reported in the text.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization and navigability.* The paper follows the standard ER feature layout and is easy to move through. Its main structural weakness is that the analyses a skeptical reader most needs (exposure distributions, switcher counts, attrition, placebo crimes, radius sensitivity, heterogeneity) are all in the online supplement. The main-text Sensitivity section (p.9) is a one-paragraph list of conclusions with no estimates. Two smaller structural problems make navigation harder. First, the Discussion presents results that never appeared in Results: the robbery "negative effect" and the specific radius thresholds (p.10). Second, the Limitations section also carries implications and generalizability material (p.11). The supplement numbering starts at Appendix Table 2 and Appendix Figure 2. The main text never cites an Appendix Table 1 or Appendix Figure 1. Readers looking for them should not assume anything is missing, but the numbering is odd, and I could not check the supplement.

*Fidelity of argument.* Table 2 is reported mostly accurately, apart from two SE mismatches. The problems are in the time-window narrative and in the mechanism language. (i) The social-emotional story shifts between Results and Discussion, and the Discussion version conflicts with Figure 2 (details below). (ii) The paragraph contrasting persistent classroom effects with transient child effects (p.10) conflicts with the preceding paragraph and with Figure 2. It also compares windows that are not comparable: the classroom model excludes the 7-day window by construction (p.5), so the claim that classroom effects "last longer" rests partly on the fact that classroom effects cannot be measured at the shortest window. (iii) Mechanism language goes beyond the design. The Conclusions say the social-emotional results "provide evidence that classroom quality may be a mechanism" (p.11), and the Results say additional homicides "cause worse between-child interactions" (p.7). No mediation analysis is reported. The between-child-interaction item is not among the two items the text itself calls statistically significant (p.7). (iv) The Discussion says the motor null "matches our initial hypothesis" (p.10), but the hypothesis on p.2 predicted negative effects on child development generally. (v) The Discussion cites Ang (2021) as showing that "the effects of exposure to homicides" are detectable within 0.5 miles of home (p.10). The paper's own reference list titles that study "The effects of police violence on inner-city students" (p.12), which is a narrower exposure than homicides in general.

*Abstract fidelity.* The abstract gets the design and the classroom headline (–.53 SD; the sign is implied by "reduce") mostly right. It leaves out the facts readers need to calibrate: the effects are per additional homicide within 500 m; the windows differ (7 days for children, 14 for classrooms); the sample is 298 children and 52 classrooms. It also omits the imprecision of the classroom estimate (SE 0.26, p ≈ .04). Its child range (–.14 to –.35) spans a null (motor) and leaves out a positive coefficient (executive functions). The claim that effects are "particularly in classrooms with fewer baseline resources" rests on a supplementary table with no numbers in the text. "Effects detectable up to 6 weeks" matches the significant 42-day estimate in Figure 3, but does not mention that the 21-day estimate is null.

*Tables and figures.* Table 2 is exemplary in layout. Its note, however, describes only the child specification: the chronic window is "8 and 97 days prior to child assessments," and it never mentions the "center-level structural quality indicators" that p.5 says the classroom model includes. Table 1 has three problems. (a) The note says "Units are expressed in standard deviations," but the table reports proportions (0.45 female), months (45.35), and years (28.17), so readers cannot tell whether an "unadjusted difference" of 0.91 for age is in months or SDs. (b) FE-adjusted differences are exactly 0.00 for time-invariant child traits (female, age), as they must be. Yet they are nonzero for caregiver education (–0.07), mother's age (–0.10), and household adults (–0.37), which are presented as baseline characteristics, and the text does not explain why. (c) For four rows (caregiver education, mother's age, household adults, teacher education), the 7-day "Unexposed M/SD" equals the full analytic-sample M/SD to two decimals, which is possible only if the exposed group is very small. Readers cannot resolve this without the data. Figure 2 has a consistent y-scale across panels but is rotated and unlabeled. I verified by zooming that its stars agree with Table 2 at the 7-day window (numeracy \*\*\*, literacy \*\*, social-emotional \*). Figures 3 and 4 are clear and labeled, although their notes and axis titles say "assessment" for what is a classroom observation date. The Figure 1 note ("black bolts in a red box") matches the map: black bolts on orange-red squares.

*Density.* At 13 pages the paper is lean. The main risk of skimming is taking the prose's numerical summaries at face value, which this review advises against.

**Checkable discrepancies** (each verified against the rendered page):

1. p.6, Results text: numeracy SE = 0.05 / p.7, Table 2, col. 1: SE = (0.06).
2. p.7, Results text: pedagogical-quality SE = 0.25 / p.7, Table 2, col. 6: SE = (0.26).
3. p.1, Abstract: child effects "ds = –.14 SD to –.35 SD" / p.7, Table 2, cols. 1–5: –0.35\*\*\*, –0.28\*\*, –0.14 (n.s.), –0.34\*, +0.12 (n.s.). The lower end of the range is a null, and a positive coefficient is excluded.
4. pp.6–7, Results text: social-emotional effects –0.28 to –0.34 SD "within 35 days ... only become null for longer windows" / p.8, Figure 2 (Socioemotional): 14-day estimate ≈ –0.10, CI crosses zero, no star.
5. p.10, Discussion: social-emotional "long-lived effect ... up to 42 days ... ranging from –0.11 SD to –0.33 SD" / p.8, Figure 2: 42-day estimate ≈ –0.07, not significant. Significant estimates appear only at 7, 21, 28, and 35 days.
6. pp.6–7, Results: social-emotional range –0.28 to –0.34, within 35 days / p.10, Discussion: –0.11 to –0.33, up to 42 days (text vs. text).
7. p.10, Discussion paragraph 3: long-lived social-emotional effects / p.10, Discussion paragraph 4: "we do not observe statistically significant child-level effects for more distant exposures." Both conflict with p.8, Figure 2: significant social-emotional estimates at –21, –28, and –35, and significant executive-function estimates at –21, –28, and –42.
8. p.4, text: differences "are substantially reduced when adjusting for within-child variation" / p.3, Table 1: learning materials, unadjusted 0.51\* vs. FE-adjusted –0.63\* (7-day) and –0.60\*\*\* vs. –0.84\*\*\* (14-day); teacher higher education, 0.24\*\* vs. –0.47\*\*\* (7-day) and –0.17\* vs. –0.36\*\*\* (14-day).
9. p.3, Table 1 note: "Units are expressed in standard deviations" / p.3, Table 1 body: proportions (female 0.45), months (age 45.35), years (mother's age 28.17).
10. p.2, Introduction: hypothesis that homicides "will negatively affect ... child development" / p.10, Discussion: the motor null "matches our initial hypothesis."
11. p.5, "Fixed effects" subsection: child FE for child outcomes and classroom FE for classroom outcomes only / p.7, Table 2 note: "child and weekday of the assessment fixed effects." Figure 2–4 notes (pp.8–9) also list "assessment weekday."
12. p.5, Analytic Approach: the classroom model includes "center-level structural quality indicators" / p.7, Table 2 note: controls listed as months between collections plus homicides 8–97 days prior to *child* assessments only.
13. p.4, Measures: shock windows "7, 14, 21, 28, 35, and 42 days" / p.5 ("windows that range from 1 to 7 weeks"), p.6, and Figures 2–4 (pp.8–9): windows run to –49 days.
14. p.5, Analytic Approach: "60 children were exposed within the prior 2 weeks at one wave but not at another" / p.7, Table 2 note a: the child headline predictor uses a 7-day window. No switcher count for the headline window is given in the main text.
15. p.2, Sample: 298 children in the analytic sample (× 2 waves = 596) and 52 classrooms (× 2 = 104) / p.7, Table 2: N = 557 (child) and 102 (classroom). The main text never reconciles these. This is not necessarily an error, since the p.4–5 exclusion rule may account for the child gap.
16. p.7, Results text: Figure 4 shows "the overall quality of activities" / p.9, Figure 4 note and p.7, Table 2, col. 7: "overall number of activities."
17. p.9, Sensitivity: effects "remain stable up to distances of 800 ms" / p.10, Discussion: "similar point estimates between 300 m and 600 m, with effects approaching zero as the exposure radius increases," diminishing to zero "between 800 m and 850 m." The two describe the same exhibit differently, and p.9 has a unit typo.
18. p.10, Discussion: "we find a negative effect related to robberies" / p.11, Limitations: "our outcomes are not affected by nonviolent crimes." p.9 calls the same exhibit "nonlethal robberies" and p.6 calls it "property crimes."
19. p.7, Results: "future homicides ... are not consistently predictive" / p.8, Figure 2: significant placebo coefficients at +14 for numeracy (≈ –0.11, \*) and executive functions (≈ –0.16, \*). This is not a contradiction, but the text does not disclose it.
20. p.7, Results: the items for "connecting content" and "announcing transitions" are the significant items / p.7, same paragraph: "additional homicides cause worse between-child interactions," a causal claim about an item not named as significant (text vs. text; Appendix Figure 3 not available).
21. p.5, Analytic Approach: "ECECs" / elsewhere: "ECEPs" (typo). p.8, Figure 2 note: "ordinary leas squares" (typo).
22. p.11, Limitations: tests that "the running variable was not manipulated" / pp.5–6, design: a two-wave fixed-effects (first-difference) design with no running variable.
23. p.12, References: the Burdick-Will (2016) entry has no journal, volume, pages, or DOI, and its venue field ("Neighborhood Violence and Academic Growth") repeats title words.
24. p.7, Table 2 title: "... on Children's Outcomes" / p.7, Table 2 body: cols. 6–7 are classroom outcomes.

Checked and found consistent: the numeracy, literacy, and social-emotional star levels in Figure 2 at –7 match Table 2. Executive functions are significant at 3, 4, and 6 weeks (p.7) as shown in Figure 2. My reading of the graph puts the 28-day point near 0.21–0.22, slightly above the stated 0.18–0.20, but Figure 2 has no labels, so I do not count this as a discrepancy. The pedagogical-quality range –0.37 to –0.60 (p.7) and "0.37 SD to 0.6 SD" (p.9) agree with each other and with Figure 3's labels. The abstract's age and sex figures (45.35 months; 45%) match Table 1. The enrolled-sample age (45.8, p.2) refers to a different sample (N = 373). The Figure 1 note matches the map.
